content.title: About
content.content: Steamed bass fillet is a tender piece of low‑fat fish rich in protein. Steaming preserves the natural flavor, aroma, and most nutrients, making it a light and healthy dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bass is a freshwater fish found in rivers and lakes across North America and Europe.
Steaming is one of the healthiest cooking methods for fish because it requires no added fat.
Bass meat is a good source of omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart and brain health.
In many traditional cuisines, bass is served with lemon and herbs to highlight its delicate taste.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Bass fillet provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Steaming keeps the fat content low, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Bass contains EPA and DHA, which promote cardiovascular health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The fish supplies B12, B6, and niacin, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Bass provides selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, supporting immunity and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including bass.

items.title: Heavy metal contamination
items.content: Like other fish, bass can contain trace amounts of mercury or other heavy metals; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the fillet has been pre‑marinated, sodium levels may be higher, which should be considered on low‑salt diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steamed bass fillet can be served with lemon, fresh herbs, soy sauce, or a light yogurt‑based sauce. It slices easily for adding to salads, rice bowls, or vegetable dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked steamed fillet in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Mussels are marine bivalve mollusks that live in coastal waters of oceans and seas. They have tender flesh, a delicate sea flavor and a slightly sweet aroma. Mussels are usually eaten cooked – boiled, steamed or baked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mussels filter water, cleaning it of microscopic particles and bacteria.
There are over 3,000 species of mussels, but the blue and green mussel (Mytilus edulis) is the most common in cuisine.
Mussels can quickly repair damaged shells.
In ancient Roman cuisine mussels were a delicacy served with wine sauce.
Mussels can form massive beds called "mussel reefs" that stretch for kilometers.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Mussels provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, making them an excellent source of complete protein.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many seafoods, mussels contain very little fat, suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for blood formation and nerve function; mussels supply over 100 % of the daily value per 100 g.

items.title: Contain iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Mussels provide EPA and DHA, which promote heart and brain health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mussels, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Toxin contamination
items.content: Mussels can accumulate toxins (e.g., domoic acid) during harmful algal blooms; purchase only from reputable sources.

items.title: Foodborne infections
items.content: Raw or undercooked mussels may contain Vibrio bacteria, causing food poisoning.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Mussels are naturally high in sodium; people monitoring salt intake should consider this.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mussels are typically cooked in boiling water or broth for 3–5 minutes until the shells open. They can be added to soups, paella, pasta, risotto, or served with a butter‑garlic‑wine sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh mussels are kept in the refrigerator in a tightly sealed container covered with a damp cloth, and used within 1–2 days. Frozen mussels should be stored at –18 °C and consumed within 3 months. Discard any mussels with shells that do not close after a gentle tap.

content.title: About
content.content: Singapore Sling is a classic cocktail created in 1915 by bartender Harry Wong (often credited to Ngiam Tong Boon) at the Raffles Hotel in Singapore. It blends gin, cherry brandy, vermouth, blackcurrant liqueur, pineapple juice, lime juice, grenadine and bitters, delivering a bright fruity flavor with a subtle bitter edge.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original recipe contained only gin, cherry brandy and vermouth; the other ingredients were added later.
The drink gained worldwide fame after appearing in the 1988 film “Cocktail”.
It is traditionally served in a tall glass over ice, garnished with a cherry, a pineapple wedge and a sprig of mint.
Many variations exist, but the “Raffles” version is considered the canonical recipe.
In 2015, to celebrate the cocktail’s centenary, the Raffles Hotel opened a dedicated Singapore Sling Bar.

items.title: Vitamin C from pineapple and lime juice
items.content: The juices provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Antioxidants from cherry brandy and grenadine
items.content: Fruit liqueurs contain polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Moderate consumption may promote relaxation
items.content: Alcohol in moderate amounts can reduce stress and improve mood.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: Excessive alcohol intake can lead to health problems, dependence, and increased injury risk.

items.title: Sugar
items.content: The cocktail is high in sugar from grenadine and fruit juices, which may be an issue for people with diabetes or weight concerns.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to pineapple, citrus, or other components.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Serve Singapore Sling in a tall glass over ice, garnish with a cherry, a pineapple slice and a mint sprig. Sip slowly to appreciate its complex aroma and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store opened juices and liqueurs in the refrigerator. Mixed cocktail is best enjoyed immediately, as melting ice dilutes the drink and alters its taste.
